1. What are the molecular underpinnings of survival in global change conditions?

https://www.diark.org/diark/species_list/Acartia_tonsa

Copepods are one of the most abundant animals on planet. Calenoid copepods, particularly in the genus Acartia, are critical for ecosystem functioning and biogeochemical cycling. They are primary consumers at the base of the oceanic food chain, eating phytoplankton and transferring the energy up the food chain starting with larval fish. With the rapidly rising temperatures in the ocean, it is critical to understand how such ecologically important species will tolerate these changes.

Acartia tonsa is a globally distributed estuarine and near-shore coastal species found along east Coast of the US. In a number of studies described below, we’ve found that A. tonsa has the capacity to rapidly adapt to global change conditions using both genetic and epigenetic variation, i.e., using both genetic and plastic mechanisms. However, what about their cold-adapted sister species, Acartia hudsonica?! A. hudsonica is a “cold-adapted” estuarine and near-shore coastal species. It is most abundant along the New England coast (ME, NH, MA, RI, CT), generally not further south than the Chesapeake Bay and not further north than Laborador/Newfoundland, Canada. They are particularly interesting because they experience huge swings in temperature across the seasons, thus they may have high plasticity, i.e., physiological flexibility. However, they typically experience much lower temperatures on average, thus their tolerance for elevated temperatures is lower than their sister species, A. tonsa.

In addition, there are two other major gaps in knowledge: we have never measured the initial plastic and long-term evolved responses in a single experiment. Nor have we measured gene expression responses to multiple environmental stressors.

In a collaboration with colleagues at the University of Connecticutt and with funding from the National Science Foundation (2016-2019), we have carried out long-term experimental evolution studies in high temperature and low pH in these two Acartiid species to understand their capacity for and mechanisms of resilience. We have measured phenotypic, allelic, epi-allelic, and transcriptomic responses across the generations in full factorial and reciprocal transplant experiments. Below is a summary of what we have learned thus far.

  • A. tonsa can rapidly adapt to high to high temperature, low pH, and the combination, but with long-term costs revealed after 25 generations (Dam et al. 2021 Nature Climate Change).
  • Looking at the allelic responses to selection in A. tonsa, warming was the dominant driver of evolution in the combined warming and acidification treatment. However, the combination was highly synergistic with 47% of the selection response being unique from either treatment alone (Brennan et al. 2022 PNAS). These results highlight the challenge that concurrent stressors impose on predictions of adaptation to complex environmental changes.
  • In a reciprocal transplant study in A. tonsa, we found that transcriptional plasticity was lost after 15 generations of experimental evolution in global change conditions, but there was sustained genetic capacity to re-adapt to ancestral ambient conditions at the expense of genetic diversity (Brennan et al. 2022 Nature Communications).
  • A. hudsonica can also rapidly adapt to high temperature, low pH, and the combination, but with reduced survival revealed after 11 generations (~ one year) (deMayo et al. 2023 Proc. Roy. Soc. B).
  • We recently showed that both epigenetic and genetic changes seem to play a role in adaptation to global change conditions in these copepods across 25 generations (Brennan et al. 2025 PNAS; read press release here).
  • We’ve also shown that these copepods can achieve a boost in their thermal tolerance in just one generation – as beneficial as three or >40 generations (Ashlock et al. 2024 Ecology & Evolution).

Unpublished RNAseq data from an amazing A. hudsonica experiment

We measured gene expression of the experimentally evolved A. hudsonica across 12 generations in four sets of conditions:

  1. Ambient (AM; 13 degrees C, 400 micro-atm pCO2)
  2. Ocean Warming (OW; 15 degrees C, 400 micro-atm pCO2)
  3. Ocean Acidification (OA; 13 degrees C, 1000 micro-atm pCO2)
  4. Ocean Warming and Acidification (OWA; 15 degrees C; 1000 micro-atm pCO2)

Additional experimental details:

  • Animals were collected from the Long Island Sound, CT and reared in the lab for 3 generations before the start of the experiment.
  • For each treatment, there were three replicate vessels with ~4,000 individuals per vessel.
  • To sample for RNA, pools of 50 adults were taken at the end of the F0, F2, F4, and F11 generations. Water was removed and animals were flash frozen in liquid nitrogen.
  • RNA was extracted using a modified TRIzol extraction protocol.
  • Library preparation and sequencing was carried out by Novogene using standard Illumina RNAseq library prep protocols (TruSeq3).
  • Samples were sequenced 150 base pair paired-end reads (2 x 150bp) using the Illumina Novoseq 6000 platform with >20 M paired end reads per sample (20 million reads * 2 pairs * 150 base pairs per read = >6 billion base pairs of data per sample!).
  • Fun fact: If we printed our 6 billion bases as 12-point text in a single line, the sequence would stretch about 12,700 km, nearly the diameter of Earth, or back and forth across the US three times, or from Vermont to South America, or…. considering all 38 of our samples, our data would get to the moon and back!

3. The general workflow for analyzing gene expression data (Transcriptomics pipeline):

Clean the raw sequence data (Done!)

  • FastP on raw reads –> cleaned reads

Generate and annotate a de novo reference transcriptome assembly (Done!)

  • Used Trinity
  • Evaluated transcriptome assembly for quality (length and completeness) using BUSCO.

Map the clean reads to the reference assembly (Done!)

  • Use Salmon to simulateously map reads to reference transcriptome and quantify abundance.

Test for differential expression among groups (Here’s where we start!)

  • Import the data into DESeq2 in R for data normalization, visualization, and statistical tests for differential gene expression.

Perform more advanced analyses (This is us!)

  • Identify clusters of genes with correlated expression using Weighted Gene Correlation Network Analysis (WGCNA).
  • Test for functional enrichment among genes differentially expressed between groups using TopGO or GO Mann-Whitney U GO_MWU

4. What does raw Illumina sequence data look like?!

fastq

The sequence data files have the suffix .fastq (or .fq). With paired end sequencing there are two files per sample (left and right reads, _1.fq.gz, _2.fq.gz). Each file has a series of four lines for each read that includes:

  1. Sequence identifier (read name)
  2. Nucleotide sequence (A, T, G, C, and sometimes N)
  3. Separator line (usually just +)
  4. Quality scores for each base

For example:

@LH00891:141:235L3LLT3:7:1101:13675:1048 1:N:0:CGTACTAG+AGGCTTAG
ANCCATGCATGTGCCAAGTTAGAGAGACTACGAGAGGCTCATTAAAACATATCAACTTGATCGAATAG
+
I#IIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIIII

We can check out the reads using zcat FILENAME.fq.gz | head -n 4. Recall that letters early in the alphabet indicate good quality on the ASCII score. The Phred Q score is translated to ASCII characters so that a two digit number can be represented by a single character.

 Quality encoding: !"#$%&'()*+,-./0123456789:;<=>?@ABCDEFGHI
                   |         |         |         |         |
    Quality score: 0........10........20........30........40

If P is the probability that a base call is an error, then: Q = -10*log10(P)

So:

Phred Quality Score Probability of incorrect base call Base call accuracy
10 1 in 10 90%
20 1 in 100 99%
30 1 in 1000 99.9%
40 1 in 10,000 99.99%
